Complete Empirical Research Plan  

------------------------------------------------------------  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Cross-sectional two-stage least squares (2SLS) with historical instruments.  

Why IV?  
• The core regressor – quality of contemporary institutions – is simultaneously determined with income (reverse causality) and is correlated with unobservables (omitted-variable bias).  
• The colonial past furnishes plausibly exogenous shocks to institutional formation that long pre-date modern economic outcomes.  
• Unlike DID or RDD, there is no clearly dated universal “event’’ and institutional quality evolves slowly; panel variation is limited.  
• Classic event-study/DID designs would mix institutional change with contemporaneous shocks, whereas the IV strategy isolates persistent cross-sectional variation.  

Main instrument set  
a) Log settler mortality circa 17-19th century (Curtin 1989, AJR 2001)  
b) Percentage of European population in 1900 (proxy for settlement)  
c) Legal origin (Common-law dummy) – used only in robustness to avoid instrument proliferation.  

First-stage: these historical variables predict the durability of inclusive vs. extractive colonial institutions, which map into today’s protection from expropriation, rule-of-law indices, constraints on executive, etc.  

Second-stage: regress (log) GDP per capita 2015 (or 10-year average) on predicted institutional quality controlling for geography and integration.  

------------------------------------------------------------  

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable (endogenous):  
Inst_i = averaged 2000-2015 value of Worldwide Governance Indicator “Rule of Law’’ (or Polity constraints on executive) – higher values = better institutions. Continuous.

Instrument-induced “treatment’’: countries where colonial conditions fostered settlement (low mortality) are “encouraged’’ to have high Inst_i; high-mortality colonies are “encouraged’’ to have low Inst_i.  

Control group / counterfactual: countries whose historical environment discouraged European settlement and thus received extractive institutions serve as the control. Countries never colonised enter analysis but are flagged; results replicated excluding them.  

Timing: Instruments measured pre-1900, well before modern outcomes. No specific event date required for IV.  

------------------------------------------------------------  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Instrument relevance: Historical settler mortality strongly predicts current institutional quality. Plausible – well documented empirically; will test F-stat (>10).  

A2. Exclusion restriction: Conditional on latitude, continental dummies, and other geography, settler mortality influences present-day income only through institutions. Plausibility: mortality captured 19th-century disease environment not necessarily binding today; yet pathogens may have persistent human-capital effects. Address with rich geo/health controls and robustness excluding Sub-Saharan Africa.  

A3. Monotonicity / no “defiers’’: Lower mortality never led to systematically worse institutions. Historically, settlement created inclusive institutions or left them unchanged, not the reverse.  

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): One country’s colonial experience does not directly determine another’s current income, conditional on controls. Reasonable at country level.  

------------------------------------------------------------  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Direct persistence of disease environment  
   • Action: control for malaria ecology, % land within tropics, soil quality, and contemporaneous life-expectancy. Show coefficient on instrumented institutions robust.  

T2. Measurement error in institutional index  
   • Action: use multiple institutional measures (WGI, ICRG risk of expropriation, Polity) and run LIML/Fuller to lessen weak-instrument-with-noise bias.  

T3. Small sample / influential observations  
   • Action: report jackknife-IV (leave-one-out), Cook’s distance, and robust (HC2) standard errors. Replicate excluding former Neo-Europes (USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand).  

------------------------------------------------------------  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # 2SLS and robust se
library(sandwich)        # vcovHC
library(lmtest)          # coeftest

# 1. Data
dat <- fread("cross_country_institutions.csv")   # assume file exists

# 2. Variable construction
dat[, ln_gdppc  := log(gdp_per_capita_2015)]
dat[, inst_wgi  := rowMeans(.SD, na.rm = TRUE),
     .SDcols = c("rule_of_law_2000","rule_of_law_2005",
                 "rule_of_law_2010","rule_of_law_2015")]
dat[, settler_mort_ln := log(settler_mortality)]
dat[, trade_open   := (exports + imports)/gdp]
dat[, abs_lat      := abs(latitude)]
dat[, euro1900     := european_settler_share_1900]  # 0-1

# 3. Main 2SLS
iv_main <- feols(ln_gdppc ~ trade_open + abs_lat | 
                 inst_wgi ~ settler_mort_ln + euro1900,
                 data = dat, vcov = ~continent)

summary(iv_main, stage = 2)

# First-stage F-statistic
wald_iv(iv_main)

# 4. Robustness: alternative instrument (legal origin)
iv_legal <- feols(ln_gdppc ~ trade_open + abs_lat | 
                  inst_wgi ~ common_law,
                  data = dat, vcov = "hetero")

# 5. Robustness: include health controls
iv_health <- feols(ln_gdppc ~ trade_open + abs_lat + malaria_ecology |
                   inst_wgi ~ settler_mort_ln + euro1900,
                   data = dat, vcov = "hetero")
```

------------------------------------------------------------  

6. Expected Results  

Theory (North 1990, AJR 2001) predicts a sizable positive effect: moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of institutional quality (≈ 1 s.d.) should raise long-run log GDP per capita by about 0.7 – 1.0 log points (≈ 100 % increase). Geography (latitude) and trade openness will matter, but coefficient magnitudes will be smaller once institutions are instrumented.  

------------------------------------------------------------  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  

C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) .............................. 1  
C2: Exclusion plausibility (controls, theory) ........................ 0.5  
C3: No weak instrument bias after LIML check ........................ 1  
C4: Monotonicity (no institutional “defiers’’) ...................... 0.5  
C5: SUTVA / no spillovers .......................................... 1  
Total (out of 5) ................................................... 4.0  

------------------------------------------------------------
